quote: Wie ist es ferner bei einer [-x-] beliebigen Differentialgl. 2ter Ordnung z. B. $y'' = \lambda A(x) y^2 + B(x) y$
english: How is it furthermore for an arbitrary differential equation of second order, e.g. y'' = λA(x)y^2 + B(x)y?
topic: Hilbert discusses the dependence of solutions of differential equations on a parameter λ, noting that they have poles at the special values of λ, and asks general questions about singularities and branching in the parameter and about whether the coefficient A(x) is determined by the singular values.

triage.modern_statement: Context: for a linear equation such as y'' = (λA(x) + B(x))y, Hilbert notes that the relevant quantities are meromorphic in λ, with poles at the special values (eigenvalues). He also asks whether A(x) is determined by those values. His question is how far this carries over to a general second-order nonlinear equation, e.g. y'' = λA(x)y^2 + B(x)y on an interval with fixed boundary or initial data. (1) What kind of singularities does the solution, or a boundary-value functional of it, have as an analytic function of the complex parameter λ? Are they poles, or are there branch points too? (2) Can the coefficient A(x) be recovered from the set of singular or special λ-values, as in an inverse spectral problem? This is my reading of a short, open-ended note, not a precisely stated problem.
triage.answered_by: No direct answer found for this nonlinear question. Related results cover only parts of it. Poincaré (with Picard) showed that solutions of analytic ODEs depend analytically on parameters where the right-hand side is analytic. That does not settle the global singularity structure in λ for a nonlinear equation. For the linear version, the inverse question was answered: Ambarzumian (1929) for a special case, and Borg (1946), who proved that two spectra determine the potential. Later work includes Marchenko and Gelfand–Levitan. I found no source answering it for y'' = λA(x)y^2 + B(x)y. It is not one of the 23 Paris problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Poincaré–Picard theorem: solutions of ODEs depend analytically on complex parameters (local analyticity in λ where the equation is analytic).
Poincaré theorem: solutions are analytic functions of initial conditions and parameters provided the right sides of the differential equations are analytic.
Linear case: Borg (1946) proved that two spectra of a Sturm–Liouville equation uniquely determine the potential; this began inverse spectral theory.
Ambarzumian (1929) showed that the zero potential can be recovered from one spectrum; Borg (1946) proved the general foundational uniqueness theorem.

triage.why: The linear version of Hilbert's question is a classical solved topic: meromorphic dependence on the spectral parameter, plus the inverse problem settled by Borg 1946, and inverse spectral theory is still very active. The note goes further and asks about a nonlinear equation (quadratic in y, with λ multiplying the nonlinear term). Searches found only general local results (Poincaré–Picard analyticity) and linear inverse-spectral results. Nothing addressed the singularity structure in λ, or recovering A(x), for this nonlinear equation. The note is exploratory and loosely worded, so it doesn't match any named problem, and calling it 'possibly unexplored' is tentative: it may be covered in nonlinear eigenvalue or bifurcation literature that these searches missed. Whether anyone is working on it today is unclear.
